name: FTP Backdoor Exploit
short_description: Exploit the famous vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor for instant root access.
description: In 2011, an attacker inserted a backdoor into vsftpd 2.3.4's source code. When a username contains ':)' (smiley face), it opens a shell on port 6200. This is CVE-2011-2523 and one of the easiest exploits to learn with Metasploit.

steps.title: Verify the target is running
steps.explanation: This scans port 21 (FTP) and identifies the service version. Look for 'vsftpd 2.3.4'.
steps.expected: You should see: 21/tcp open ftp vsftpd 2.3.4

steps.title: Start Metasploit
steps.explanation: The -q flag skips the banner for faster startup. Wait for the msf6 > prompt.

steps.title: Search for the exploit
steps.explanation: This searches Metasploit's database for vsftpd-related modules.
steps.expected: You'll see exploit/unix/ftp/vsftpd_234_backdoor in the results

steps.title: Load the exploit module
steps.explanation: This loads the backdoor exploit. Your prompt changes to show the active module.

steps.title: View module options
steps.explanation: See what parameters the exploit needs. RHOSTS is the target IP.
steps.expected: You'll see RHOSTS is required and currently empty

steps.title: Set the target
steps.explanation: This tells Metasploit which host to attack.

steps.title: Execute the exploit
steps.explanation: This triggers the backdoor and opens a shell session.

steps.title: Verify root access (no prompt - just type!)
steps.explanation: IMPORTANT: There is NO prompt. The cursor is just blinking. Type 'whoami' and press Enter anyway - it works! Raw reverse shells don't show a prompt.

steps.title: Upgrade to a real prompt
steps.explanation: Raw reverse shells have no prompt. This spawns an interactive bash so you get a familiar root@container:/# prompt.

steps.title: Confirm full access
steps.explanation: Confirm you're root (uid=0) and can read sensitive files like /etc/shadow.

steps.title: Explore the network
steps.explanation: Docker adds container hostnames here. These are potential pivot targets.

steps.title: One-command pwn (after you learn it)
steps.explanation: Exit the shell (type 'exit' twice) and try this. Now that you understand the attack, this script runs it automatically.

success_criteria: You have a root shell with a proper prompt (root@...:#) and can explore the compromised system.
next_steps: Run 'env' to find secrets in environment variables
